items.title: James Baldwin on How Love (Finally) Finds You
items.description: Our language betrays our self-betrayals: We speak of finding love, as if it were an undiscovered eighth continent or a habitable world in another solar system, as if it got lost like the Little Red Riding Hood or the names of the women who painted the caves. Like the paradoxical notion of finding yourself, the notion of finding love pulsates with equal parts helplessness and hubris — a rueful recognition that something is missing from your life and a belief that it falls on you to do the looking

items.title: Sleeping Beauties: David Byrne on Why Transformative Ideas Fall Dormant and How They Awaken to Change the World
items.description: Each time you look up at the night sky, you see only ancient signals — by the time a photon has reached your pupil, the star that emitted it may be long dead. The great wonder is that its light can traverse immense expanses of space and time to gladden the darkness of today, to cast wonder upon this lonely planet. An idea is a signal that may travel across immense expanses of space and time before it touches the world. Transformative ideas can and often do fall on the closed eyes of their epoch.

items.title: Vincent van Gogh on Fear, Taking Risks, and How Inspired Mistakes Propel Us Forward
items.description: "However meaningless and vain, however dead life appears, the man of faith, of energy, of warmth... steps in and does something."

items.title: But We Had Music: Nick Cave Reads an Animated Poem about How to Be More Alive
items.description: How, knowing that even the universe is dying, do we bear our lives? Most readily, through friendship, through connection, through co-creating the world we want to live in for the brief time we have together on this lonely, perfect planet. The seventh annual Universe in Verse — a many-hearted labor of love, celebrating the wonder of reality through science and poetry — occasioned a joyous collaboration with Australian musician and writer Nick Cave and Brazilian artist and filmmaker Daniel Bruson

items.title: A Constellation of Amazements: An Illustrated Love Letter to the Joy of Collecting Things
items.description: We are hunter-gatherers with a capacity for amazement, wired to search for an organizing principle by which to contain the chaos of reality. We organize what we find into categories and hierarchies, hovering over which is one of the strangest things about being human: preference. How odd to have a strong feeling about a color or an object or a sequence of chords. And yet our preferences are how we sculpt the self from the monolith of the species. items.title: Elizabeth Gilbert on Love, Loss, and How to Move Through Grief as Grief Moves Through You
items.description: "Grief is a force of energy that cannot be controlled or predicted. It comes and goes on its own schedule. Grief does not obey your plans, or your wishes. Grief will do whatever it wants to you, whenever it wants to. In that regard, Grief has a lot in common with Love."

items.title: How to Remake Yourself When You Are Undone: Lincoln and the Gift of His Suicidal Depression
items.description: Life-affirming inspiration from a man who knew intimately “that intensity of thought, which will some times wear the sweetest idea thread-bare and turn it to the bitterness of death.”

items.title: How to Doubt Your Way into a Truer Life
items.description: The most maddening thing about life is also the most beautiful: its indeterminacy. The course of our lives, the fate of our species, the future of the universe: all undecided. But because possibility is the hardest thing to bear, we sedate ourselves with certainty — even though we know that liminality is the most generative place, that to believe is to doubt, that we are most creative when we attempt what is not certain. items.title: Dostoyevsky on What Makes a Good Person
items.description: We know good people when we encounter them, when they fall upon our lives like a sunbeam, like a song. But we don’t always know what makes them good. It has, of course, a lot to do with kindness. It has to do with their capacity to give, and also to receive. It has to do with their courage of uncertainty. items.description: "We are our memory… that chimerical museum of shifting shapes, that pile of broken mirrors.”

items.title: Why Are We Not Better Than We Are
items.description: "...a stillness in which the germ of what is not yet palpable pauses and gathers to begin one more time."

items.description: "Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?"

items.description: Inside the brain's secret portal to remembering the future.

items.title: Walt Whitman, Shortly After His Paralytic Stroke, on What Makes Life Worth Living
items.description: "Tone your wants and tastes low down enough, and make much of negatives, and of mere daylight and the skies."
